items.title: Cognitive load theory shapes instructional design
items.claim: John Sweller's cognitive load theory (1988 onwards) distinguishes three types of load. Which design principle follows directly?

options.text: Always make instructions as long as possible

Minimise extraneous load (poor design) and manage intrinsic load (task complexity) so working memory can devote capacity to germane load (schema formation) — worked examples for novices, problem-solving for experts (expertise reversal effect)

items.reveal_title: Working memory is the bottleneck for learning
items.reveal:
Sweller's theory builds on Miller's 7+/-2 and Baddeley's working memory. Educational applications include worked-example effect (better than problem-solving for novices), modality effect (combining visual + auditory exceeds visual alone), redundancy effect (repeating information harms learning).

David Geary distinguishes 'biologically primary' knowledge (language, faces) that we acquire effortlessly from 'biologically secondary' (reading, algebra) that requires designed instruction. The theory has reshaped UK curriculum guidance (EEF 2018, Ofsted 2019).
items.why: Teaching that ignores working memory limits — long instructions, complex diagrams, novice problem-solving — is measurably less effective. CLT puts a constraint into instructional design.

items.title: CBT works for depression — with caveats
items.claim: Cuijpers and colleagues' meta-analyses of CBT for depression report effect sizes in the moderate range. What's the most important methodological caveat?

options.text: Most trials have substantial risk of bias (publication bias, lack of blinding, allegiance effects when researchers favour the treatment); effect sizes may be inflated by 20-50%
CBT only works for healthy people

items.reveal:
Pim Cuijpers's group has published numerous meta-analyses (Cuijpers et al. 2010, 2014, 2019). They consistently find CBT and other structured psychotherapies effective for depression but with methodological caveats: many trials are not blinded (impossible for psychotherapy), researcher allegiance correlates with effect size, publication bias remains an issue.

The NHS's IAPT (Improving Access to Psychological Therapies, 2008) made CBT widely available; routine outcomes data show recovery rates around 50% within treatment, lower than RCTs.
items.why: Treatment efficacy is layered: works in trials, sometimes less well in routine practice. The research-practice gap matters for service planning.

items.title: Choking is more than just nerves
items.claim: Sian Beilock and colleagues' research on choking under pressure identifies two mechanisms. Which?

options.text: Distraction (anxiety occupies working memory needed for the task) and explicit monitoring (conscious attention to automatic motor skills disrupts them) — different mechanisms suggest different interventions

items.reveal:
Beilock and Carr (2001, 2005) showed expert golfers putted worse when paying conscious attention to their swing; novices benefited from explicit instruction.

Distraction-based choking responds to attention training and pre-performance routines; monitoring-based choking responds to maintaining flow-state distraction (focusing on external targets rather than mechanics). The dual-process model has reshaped elite athlete preparation.
items.why: Choking has identifiable mechanisms with specific countermeasures. Generic 'stay calm' advice misses both.
